Also flagged as a related hardening item regardless of approach: the deployed app auto-commits/pushes trip_log.csv on every log action - if both anglers log a catch at the same moment from separate devices, the second push could get rejected (non-fast-forward) the way we saw during a manual push tonight; the app's own auto-commit logic should pull-rebase-push with a retry so a genuinely simultaneous log from two phones never silently fails.

SOMEDAY/MAYBE - not for now, captured for later reference. Scoped after discussing true offline field-logging (dead-zone signal on the lake) and the possibility of eventually making this a public app with an upgraded look and feel. Confirmed Streamlit has no offline/PWA support at all (every interaction is a live round trip to the Python server - no official PWA toolkit, community consensus is it's not feasible) and that iOS Safari doesn't support the Background Sync API, so a real offline-capable field app means leaving Streamlit for a native/cross-platform mobile app (React Native or Flutter - one codebase for iOS+Android), with a local on-device database (SQLite) for full offline read/write and sync-on-reconnect, matching how real offline field-data tools (ODK Collect, ArcGIS Field Maps, Fulcrum) are all built as native apps, not web apps, for exactly this reason. Going public compounds the rebuild: (1) data layer - replace trip_log.csv-in-git with a real database (e.g. Postgres via Supabase/Neon) for genuine concurrent multi-user writes, real user accounts/auth replacing both Streamlit's lack of auth and the 'who's fishing' name tag, and a real API layer (FastAPI is a natural fit - the existing core/ scoring, lure, and weather logic is plain Python with no Streamlit dependency, so most of it carries over behind API endpoints rather than being rewritten); (2) the mobile app itself - offline-first field logging, camera/GPS via native APIs instead of browser widgets, app-store distribution and review cycles; (3) a separate public web frontend (real design system instead of Streamlit's default widget styling) for browsing forecasts/trip history without installing an app; (4) public-readiness hardening - rate limits/caching on external calls (Open-Meteo, USGS, USACE, Cabela's lookup, Claude vision lure-scanner) that are currently fine for 2 users but need real per-user caps at scale, real (non-free) hosting/ops, a privacy policy given anglers are protective of their spot locations, and a scope decision on single-lake (everything right now - bathymetry, shoreline, fish attractors - is Nolin-specific data) vs. multi-lake support. This is a genuine rebuild done as a different kind of project - months not days, with real staging/production environments and app-store release cycles - not an incremental feature on top of the current app. Revisit this item if/when ready to actually scope and start it.

Leaderboard periodically showed stale data, and a Streamlit Cloud reboot corrected it - twice. Root cause: get_trip_history()/get_calibrated_weights() (core/appstate.py, both a 5-minute st.cache_data) are read by Leaderboard, 7-Day Forecast, and Spot Session's own lure-recommendation panels, but unlike every other cached getter in this app (get_lake_spots, get_inventory, get_dev_tasks - each cleared right after its own page's write), neither was ever cleared after a trip write anywhere, across all 9 write sites in pages/6_Spot_Session.py and pages/4_Trip_History.py. A reboot masked this by starting a fresh process with a fresh cache. Fixed by clearing both caches at every write site (centralized in Spot Session's _push_or_toast() helper), and added a matching Refresh from GitHub button to Leaderboard (Trip History's existing one now clears these caches too, not just re-syncing the file). Separately confirmed: this morning's live session was lost the same way as the prior incident - the angler's reboot was a genuine Streamlit Cloud restart, which replaced the process's disk before that session's data ever reached GitHub. No written record exists; recreating from memory is in progress.

After swapping in a fresh PAT and rebooting, verified via a real Start Session / Cancel Session test that pushes still weren't reaching GitHub - zero new commits on the data branch, no visible toast either time. Root cause: github_token() reads st.secrets and returns empty on ANY problem (missing key, typo, a TOML syntax error elsewhere breaking the whole parse) with no signal beyond an easy-to-miss toast - so 'no token configured' and 'token configured but I can't tell' were indistinguishable from the UI. Added core.appstate.github_connection_status() and a persistent (not a toast) connection-status line on Spot Session (top of page) and Development (in an expander) - green + masked token preview if github_token() sees one, orange/red warning if not - so this is always checkable without depending on catching a toast. Separately, the Cancel Session confirm needing two clicks to take effect could not be reproduced in an isolated AppTest run of the exact click sequence (cancels correctly on the first confirm click every time) - left open as a likely client-side/network timing issue pending the token fix being confirmed.

Re-ran the Start/Cancel Session test with the new punch-list #62 connection indicator visible the whole time - it stayed 'connected' throughout, yet the push still never reached GitHub (confirmed via git log on the data branch: no new commits) and the Cancel Session double-click issue persisted. Root cause of the false confidence: github_connection_status() only checks whether github_token() returns a non-empty string - it can't distinguish a garbage/revoked/wrong-scope token from a genuinely working one, since that requires an actual round trip to GitHub. Added core.appstate.test_github_push_access(token, slug) - a real on-demand GitHub API request against the repo, interpreting the response the same way this session diagnosed the two previous bad tokens by hand with curl (401 = invalid/revoked, 200 with permissions.push: false = valid but read-only, permissions.push: true = genuinely working). Wired into a new 'Test connection now' button in Development's GitHub connection expander.

Live-tested the reported "pushes never reach GitHub despite a valid, push-capable token" and "Cancel Session needs two clicks" issues directly on the deployed app via browser automation (the angler asked me to reproduce them myself rather than keep relying on descriptions). A background fragment's periodic auto-rerun landing near a click on an unrelated button is a known way for that click to get silently dropped.
